props.title: Valley of the Dolls

sections.content: **Valley of the Dolls** (1967) blazed a scandalous trail through Hollywood, adapting Jacqueline Susann's explosive novel about prescription drug addiction and showbiz destruction. The film follows three women - Anne Welles (Barbara Parkins), Neely O'Hara (Patty Duke), and Jennifer North (Sharon Tate) - as they spiral into dependency on "dolls" (prescription pills) while chasing fame. Its gaudy melodrama and camp performances, particularly Duke's over-the-top portrayal, transformed it from intended serious drama into an accidental cult classic. The film shares DNA with **What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?** (1962) in its grotesque portrayal of Hollywood's treatment of women, though with a distinctly psychedelic late-60s aesthetic.

sections.content: The film's influence on depicting addiction and celebrity culture rippled through later works like **Boogie Nights** (1997) and **Black Swan** (2010). Its particular brand of heightened melodrama and fashion excess created a template for "women in peril" films that followed, including **Looking for Mr. Goodbar** (1977) and **Star 80** (1983). The tragic real-life murder of Sharon Tate two years after the film's release added another layer of dark mythology to its legacy. SUBHEAD: The Camp Legacy

While initially panned by critics, **Valley of the Dolls** (1967) found new life as a camp masterpiece, inspiring drag performances and midnight screenings alongside films like **Mommie Dearest** (1981) and **Showgirls** (1995). Its quotable dialogue ("Sparkle, Neely, sparkle!") and exaggerated performances created a blueprint for intentional camp films like **The Rocky Horror Picture Show** (1975). The film's costume design by Travilla, who famously dressed Marilyn Monroe, influenced fashion-forward films from **Mahogany** (1975) to **The Devil Wears Prada** (2006).
